messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia was thirty-three, a network engineer who spent her days managing server rooms and virtual private networks, a job that demanded precision and calm. But the calm had been gone for years. It had evaporated the moment her four-year-old daughter, Leilani, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of leukemia. Malia remembered the fluorescent lights of the pediatric ICU, the way doctors spoke in clipped syllables, the endless beeping of monitors. She remembered the arguments—with her husband at the time, who wanted to pursue alternative treatments, with her mother, who questioned every medical decision. Treatment worked. Leilani was now eight, in remission, a happy, healthy child who had no memory of the worst months. But her mother remembered everything.

Two years after Leilani’s recovery, Malia’s marriage dissolved. She did not fight it. The divorce was quiet, almost relief, because the arguments had become unbearable—each one reopened the hospital room, the helplessness, the fear. Even now, a disagreement with a colleague about a cable routing protocol could send her heart racing. Her body remembered before her mind did: the sudden heat under her collar, the shallow breath, the tremor in her hands. It was not anger she felt. It was something older, a sense that the world was about to shatter again.

She had learned to stay away from known people—friends from her old life, relatives who asked too many questions. She kept her distance from her ex-husband, only texted about drop-offs. She had come to believe that any close relationship carried the risk of another catastrophe, and so she maintained a polite, functional isolation. Her colleagues knew her as efficient but distant. No one came to her desk unannounced. That was the rule.

But the vigilance did not stay at work. At home, in her small apartment, Malia could not settle. She felt on guard even when the door was locked and the blinds were drawn. A floorboard creak—her neighbor, she knew—and she would freeze, scanning the room. Unexpected movement nearby, even a cat darting past the window, made her flinch as if a needle were sliding into her arm. The medical procedures she had endured alongside Leilani—the blood draws, the spinal taps—had become a permanent trigger. Now, when she herself needed a routine physical or a mammogram, the anticipation would build for days. The sight of a stethoscope was enough to cause a wave of nausea and a pounding pulse, and she often cancelled appointments and rescheduled, then cancelled again.

The more on edge she remained, the more she noticed potential threats—and the more arguments she provoked. She had started snapping at her team lead for a minor error in a configuration file, then apologised, then felt humiliated. But the hypervigilance would not quiet. She began to avoid the break room during lunch because a coworker liked to sneak up behind people. She took her coffee at her desk, door half-closed, monitoring the hallway for any sudden movement. It was exhausting. She knew, rationally, that no one was coming for her. But the feeling in her body—the tight chest, the coiled muscles—would not listen to reason.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a simple thing: a letter from her gynecologist reminding her of a Pap smear she had missed twice. She sat at her kitchen table, the paper trembling in her hands, and realised she could not go through another cycle of avoidance and dread. She was afraid of what the exam might find—and more afraid of the terror that would accompany it. She wanted to be able to take her daughter to the doctor without reliving the worst year of her life. She wanted to stop starting arguments because her nerves were too frayed to tolerate someone else’s uncertainty. She wanted, she told the intake therapist, just to feel safe in her own body again.
